aria_snapshot:
- main:
  - text: TYPE 2 / 1950 → FOREVER
  - heading "From utility to hippie." [level=1]:
    - text: From
    - emphasis: utility
    - text: to hippie.
  - paragraph: The Volkswagen van began as a box for the working day. Its honest shape became a camper, a protest vehicle, a rolling canvas—and one of the few machines to belong equally to tradespeople and dreamers.
  - link "Ride through the story":
    - /url: "#story"
  - img "Classic split-window Volkswagen Type 2 van on the road"
  - text: THE BOX THAT WOULDN’T STAY IN ONE LANE BORN TO WORK — ADOPTED BY WANDERERS
  - heading "A blank rectangle with a thousand lives." [level=2]
  - paragraph: "Ben Pon’s 1947 sketch imagined a compact transporter built around Volkswagen mechanics. Production began in 1950. The trick was not luxury or speed: it was useful volume. With the driver over the front wheels and the engine at the rear, the space between could become almost anything."
  - strong: "1950"
  - text: first T1 Transporter enters production
  - strong: 4.6 m³
  - text: load space in the original panel van
  - strong: "1956"
  - text: Westfalia campers reach the United States
  - region "Choose a life.":
    - heading "Choose a life." [level=2]
    - paragraph: The body stayed simple; the meaning changed with whoever held the keys. Select an era to see how the same platform crossed from commerce into culture.
    - tablist "Volkswagen van eras":
      - tab "01 · Workhorse" [selected]
      - tab "02 · Weekender"
      - tab "03 · Counterculture"
      - tab "04 · Cult classic"
    - tabpanel:
      - img "Early Volkswagen Type 2 panel van used as a practical transporter"
      - text: 1950s · CLOCKED IN
      - heading "The working van." [level=3]
      - paragraph: "The earliest Type 2 was all business: panel van, Kombi, minibus and pickup. Flat sides carried names and signs; the cabin-forward layout kept a large cargo bay inside a small footprint."
      - list:
        - listitem: FOR deliveries, crews, tools
        - listitem: WHY simple, compact, adaptable
        - listitem: LOOK split windshield, V-shaped nose
  - text: same shell / new rules
  - heading "The journey from jobsite to campsite took one fold-out bed." [level=2]
  - figure "WESTFALIA-STYLE CONVERSIONS TURNED CARGO SPACE INTO A TINY HOME.":
    - img "Restored 1967 Volkswagen Type 2 camper van"
    - text: WESTFALIA-STYLE CONVERSIONS TURNED CARGO SPACE INTO A TINY HOME.
  - 'figure "CABINET, TABLE, BENCH, BED: DOMESTIC LIFE PACKED INTO A FEW FEET."':
    - img "Vintage Volkswagen Westfalia camper interior with compact cabinetry and seating"
    - text: "CABINET, TABLE, BENCH, BED: DOMESTIC LIFE PACKED INTO A FEW FEET."
  - region "How a tool became a symbol.":
    - heading "How a tool became a symbol." [level=2]
    - article:
      - time: "1947"
      - heading "The sketch" [level=3]
      - paragraph: "Dutch importer Ben Pon draws the seed of a Beetle-based transporter: maximum carrying space on a compact footprint."
    - article:
      - time: "1950"
      - heading "The T1 clocks in" [level=3]
      - paragraph: The first production Transporter leaves Wolfsburg. Panel van first; passenger and pickup variants follow quickly.
    - article:
      - time: "1956"
      - heading "The room appears" [level=3]
      - paragraph: Westfalia camper conversions reach the U.S., formalizing what owners were already doing—turning the bus into a portable life.
    - article:
      - time: 1960s
      - heading "The people repaint the meaning" [level=3]
      - paragraph: Affordable space, an unconventional silhouette and easy customization make the Microbus a natural fit for musicians, organizers, travelers and the counterculture.
    - article:
      - time: "1967"
      - heading "The bay window arrives" [level=3]
      - paragraph: The second generation trades the split windshield for a broad curved pane, better visibility and a more capable platform—without losing the friendly face.
    - article:
      - time: NOW
      - heading "The blank canvas survives" [level=3]
      - paragraph: "Restorers, campers, collectors and artists still read the same simple body as an invitation: work with it, sleep in it, paint it, go."
  - paragraph: It didn’t stop being useful when it became a hippie icon. Its usefulness is what made the freedom possible.
  - complementary:
    - heading "The real legacy" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "The van’s countercultural image can hide a wider story. Microbuses moved bands and families—but also people to rallies, polling stations and schools. Its symbolism grew from the same trait that made it a work van: it could carry people and purpose together."
